title: hashbuck-superblock-mapping-and-lightweight-defragging
body:
Summary:

This doc sketches an alternate approach to our KV-cache memory layout and background reclamation that targets two problems we keep hitting in prod: (1) high internal fragmentation due to variable-sized cached segments and (2) expensive stop-the-world compaction/pinning during tail pressure. The idea: partition the heap into fixed-size superblocks and map logical cache keys into small sub-blocks via a stable hash-bucket mapping. When fragmentation rises we run lightweight, localized defragmentation by relocating a few hot-to-warm items across bucket boundaries rather than doing large-scale compaction.

Goals:
- Reduce tail latency spikes caused by full-heap compaction.
- Keep per-request allocation/lookup hot path simple and lock-light.
- Bound memory blowups from fragmentation under churny workloads.
- Provide clear telemetry so SRE/product can set fragmentation-based alarms.

Non-goals:
- Replace slab allocator entirely (we still want some pool for tiny objects in other paths).
- Fully eliminate fragmentation — aim is to keep fragmentation within a predictable budget and avoid pathological cases.

High-level design:
1) Superblocks: global heap is split into N fixed-size superblocks (e.g., 256KB superblock). Superblocks are the unit of background relocation and coarse accounting. Each superblock contains multiple allocation slots (sub-blocks) of variable sizes but aligned to a small quantum (e.g., 64B).

2) HashBuck mapping: logical keys are hashed into buck_id = hash(key) % M, where M is number of hash buckets. Each bucket maps to an ordered list of superblock slots reserved for that bucket. The mapping is stable: a key's bucket does not change unless the system triggers a re-shard operation (rare). This provides locality and makes it easy to identify candidate relocation targets inside the same bucket.

3) Bucket-level occupancy map: each bucket maintains a compact occupancy bitmap (one bit per quantum within each mapped superblock) + a small hotness vector (sampled access counters, e.g., 8-bit saturating). These structures are read-mostly on the hot path; mutation happens on allocation/eviction.

4) Lightweight defragger: background worker that runs per-bucket. When bucket fragmentation metric exceeds threshold (see telemetry section) the worker tries to coalesce live entries into fewer superblocks by relocating a small number of entries: pick source superblocks with low aggregate hotness, select victims (largest cold entries first), copy to destination superblock (atomically swap entry pointers), then free vacated slot. Relocation is O(k) where k is small (configurable). No stop-the-world.

5) Eviction & admission: admission uses a two-tier score: score = alpha*age + beta*size_rank + gamma*hotness_decay; eviction chooses lowest score within target bucket or global under high pressure. We bias eviction to evict items that help fragmentation (i.e., large cold items that free contiguous ranges).

Memory layout details:
- Superblock size: tunable, default 256KB. Rationale: keeps bookkeeping small but enables room for a handful of medium objects.
- Quantum: 64B alignment for payloads; headers live in adjacent metadata region within the superblock, not inline with payload to keep lookups cache-friendly.
- Per-superblock header (64B): superblock id, bucket id, occupancy count, generation epoch, checksum. Kept compact and 8-byte aligned.
- Slot metadata (16B per slot): pointer to key-hash, payload-size, entry-state (active/moving/free), tombstone flag for in-flight relocations. Stored separately in a hot metadata slab to keep pointer chasing local.

Concurrency model and correctness:
- Hot path (lookup): compute bucket, probe bucket's slot list (small expected set), check slot metadata state; if state==moving, help-forward by reading relocation target pointer (CAS-free read). Fast path uses relaxed atomic loads.
- Allocation: try to allocate within bucket's mapped superblocks using first-fit in per-superblock free map. If none, attempt buck-level steal from sibling buckets (configurable) or trigger lightweight defragger. Only if all fails we fallback to global eviction.
- Relocation protocol: writer initiates move by allocating destination slot and marking source state=MOVING->dest_ptr. Writers use CAS to swap in new payload pointer in the global index (per-key pointer table). Readers observing MOVING re-resolve via dest_ptr. A small grace period and epoch counters ensure no ABA. Copy is done with write barriers to make header visible before pointer swap.

Eviction heuristics and policies:
- Localized eviction: prefer to evict within a bucket unless global memory pressure high. This maintains stable latency by avoiding cross-bucket thrashing.
- Fragmentation-aware bonus: increase eviction priority for entries whose removal would unlock >X contiguous quanta in a superblock. This helps the defragger create fewer destination write operations.
- Size-class aware: for very large values (> superblock/4) we isolate them into dedicated superblocks (big-object lanes) to avoid polluting many small slots and to simplify reclaim.

Telemetry and observability:
Expose these key metrics per-bucket and global:
- bucket_fragmentation_percent (ratio of unusable quanta due to scattering)
- superblock_free_runs_count (number of contiguous free ranges)
- avg_relocations_per_defrag_cycle
- relocation_latency_p95
- eviction_breakdown_by_reason (hotness/fragmentation/age/size)
- allocation_failures_per_minute
- bytes_moved_total
- hot_path_lookups_helped_by_forwarding

Alerting suggestion:
- page: fragmentation > 20% for 5m for >5% of buckets
- page: relocation_latency_p95 > 100ms
- warning: allocation_failures_per_minute > 5

Benchmarks & simulation plan:
- Build a micro-sim that replays request traces (real traces from prod for 24h) and compare: classic slab + best-fit, our superblock+hashbuck, and baseline buddy allocator. Metrics: tail alloc latency, bytes moved per minute, payload cache-hit-rate, fragmentation_percent.
- Target: reduce bytes moved during steady-state defrag by 50% vs full compaction; keep 99.9th alloc latency under 5ms.

Operational concerns and failure modes:
- Hash bucket skew: skewed key distribution may overload certain buckets. Mitigations: per-bucket rebalancing (move some superblocks between buckets), or dynamic M increase with gradual re-hash. Re-hash must be rare and done as background migration.
- In-flight relocation storms: if a popular key is repeatedly relocated because of racing background defraggers, we add a cool-off timestamp in metadata and boost hotness to keep hot items stable.
- Cost of metadata: per-slot metadata adds overhead; pick quantum carefully. If quantum too small, metadata overhead dominates.
- Torn writes and crash recovery: maintain per-superblock generation and write-ahead relocation state (small journal) to reconcile after crash. We want fast recovery, so journal entries are per-relocation and bounded in size.

Implementation incremental plan (MVP -> v1 -> v1.1):
MVP (4 wks):
- implement superblock allocator and fixed bucket mapping
- basic lookup/insert/evict within bucket with simple first-fit free map
- exposure of fragmentation telemetry per-bucket
- unit tests and microbench harness

v1 (6 wks):
- background lightweight defragger with relocation protocol (single-threaded per-bucket)
- fragmentation-aware eviction bonus
- run replay sim and compare with current allocator
- soak on staging for 2 weeks

v1.1 (8 wks):
- concurrent multi-threaded defragger with per-bucket worker pool
- per-bucket rebalancing to mitigate skew
- journaled relocation for crash safety
- production rollout via canary and traffic ramp

Open questions / TODOs:
- exact superblock size & quantum matrix: run sims to pick optimal tradeoff for our typical payload size distribution.
- how to integrate with existing pinned KV entries (persistent pin API) without extra copies.
- tuning knobs: default thresholds for defrag triggers vs. background CPU cost.
- eviction fairness across tenants in Dedicated clusters — need to surface per-tenant fragmentation to billing/ops.

Appendix: quick ASCII sketch of layout
[heap] -> SB0 | SB1 | SB2 | SB3 | ...
SB0 header: bucket=3 epoch=12 occupancy=18
SB0 payload area: slots -> [used][free][used][used][free free][used contiguous run]
Bucket 3 -> mapped SB0, SB5, SB17 (bitmap + hotness array)
Relocation example sequence:
1) defragger chooses SB0 -> allocate slot in SB5
2) copy payload to SB5 slot
3) write dest_ptr into SB0 slot metadata (MOVING -> dest)
4) CAS pointer in global index from old_slot -> new_slot
5) mark old_slot free and update occupancy.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally conservative: no global re-sharding in MVP, no forced compaction. We trade slightly higher background CPU for predictable latency.
- I want feedback on the relocation write ordering (barrier semantics) and whether teams prefer a per-key indirection table vs in-slot direct pointers. Indirection speeds relocate but adds one more pointer chase on hot path.

Action items before next sync:
- Priya: run trace-size distribution and produce heatmap (by key size) by 2024-10-10
- Miguel: spike on superblock=128KB vs 256KB sim by 2024-10-14
- Eva: prototype per-bucket occupancy bitmap layout and memory overhead calculation by 2024-10-18
- Jordan: draft relocation journaling format and recovery sequence by 2024-10-20

-- end of doc --
